I am working on HSE LLM4Rec Assignment A03 Week 3: Collaborative Filtering.

All files in this OpenCode project folder are the Week 3 files for this assignment.


Professor-shared Week 3 repository:
https://github.com/dryjins/RecSys-LLMs/tree/main/week3


This is STEP 1: BASELINE AUDIT BEFORE IMPLEMENTATION.




A. Rules


1. Do not rebuild the project from scratch.
2. Do not edit any file yet.
3. Do not modify u.data or u.item.
4. Do not modify readme.md.
5. Do not assume a bug exists before testing it.
6. Separate confirmed facts, hypotheses, executed tests, and conclusions.
7. Use the files inside this Week 3 project folder as the local baseline.
8. Read executable code, not only comments or README instructions.
9. Use the professor-shared Week 3 repository only as a reference for checking the starter structure if needed.
10. Do not use code, UI logic, algorithm logic, or report content from any previous homework.
11. Do not claim anything works unless you actually run or test it.
12. Do not claim browser verification unless you actually run the application in a browser.
13. Do not claim that I personally verified any calculation yet.
14. Keep this investigation clear, reproducible, and suitable for the final session.json audit trail.
15. Do not implement anything until I explicitly approve Step 2.




B. HW3 requirements to keep in scope


HW3: Collaborative Filtering


Implementation requirements:


1. Use the existing MovieLens 100K u.data and u.item files in this Week 3 project.
2. Implement User-Based Collaborative Filtering.
3. Implement Item-Based Collaborative Filtering.
4. Implement similarity calculations comparing users and items.
5. Handle sparse ratings using ONE missing-value strategy.


The assignment-level strategy choices are:


a. mean imputation
b. weighted by common ratings
c. matrix factorization


The Week 3 repository may describe a slightly different list of strategies.


If assignment material, README, comments, and starter code disagree, report the mismatch clearly.


Do not resolve the mismatch yet.


Business and algorithmic analysis requirements:


1. Compare User-Based and Item-Based recommendation quality.
2. Compare User-Based and Item-Based computational efficiency depending on the number of users and items.
3. Analyze mean imputation, weighted common-rating handling, and matrix factorization in terms of:
   a. simplicity
   b. bias
   c. computational cost
4. Explain cold-start failure for:
   a. new users with no ratings
   b. new items with no ratings
5. Explain why similarity values based on very few co-rated observations are unreliable because they have too little supporting evidence.




C. Inspect the complete Week 3 project


Read every relevant Week 3 file and report:


1. What each file does.
2. How u.item is loaded.
3. How u.item is parsed.
4. How u.data is loaded.
5. How u.data is parsed.
6. How users are represented.
7. How movies are represented.
8. How ratings are represented.
9. Whether a user-item rating matrix currently exists.
10. How missing ratings are represented.
11. What the current UI does.
12. What controls the current UI contains.
13. Whether the current UI generates Top-5 recommendations.
14. Whether the current UI predicts one selected user/movie rating.
15. What similarity functions exist.
16. Whether cosine similarity is implemented or only a placeholder.
17. Whether User-Based CF is implemented.
18. Whether Item-Based CF is implemented.
19. Whether prediction or recommendation formulas already exist.
20. Whether Top-K recommendation logic already exists.
21. Whether a missing-value strategy is currently implemented.
22. Whether cold-start handling exists.
23. Whether co-rated-count handling exists.
24. Which functions are TODOs or placeholders.
25. Which functions return 0, null, [] or other placeholder values because they are unfinished.




D. Trace the current baseline pipeline


Explain the current application flow in order:


1. Data loading.
2. Data parsing.
3. Matrix construction.
4. User selection.
5. Similarity calculation.
6. Neighbor or similar-item selection.
7. Prediction calculation.
8. Candidate filtering.
9. Sorting/ranking.
10. Top-K selection.
11. UI rendering.


If the pipeline stops because something is not implemented, identify the exact function where it stops.




E. Establish confirmed baseline facts


Using the actual local Week 3 files, determine:


1. Number of users.
2. Number of movies.
3. Number of ratings.
4. Rating scale.
5. Minimum rating.
6. Maximum rating.
7. Whether user IDs are 1-based.
8. Whether movie IDs are 1-based.
9. Whether 0 represents not rated.
10. Whether buildRatingMatrix() is implemented.
11. Whether cosineSimilarity() is implemented.
12. Whether User-Based CF currently works.
13. Whether Item-Based CF currently works.
14. Whether the current application produces Top-5 recommendations.
15. Whether the current application instead predicts one selected rating.
16. Whether missing values are currently ignored, imputed, weighted, or untreated.
17. Whether predictions or recommendation scores can currently become NaN or Infinity.
18. Whether cold-start cases are handled.
19. Whether low co-rated counts affect similarity.
20. Whether results are deterministic for identical input.




F. Compare the Week 3 sources


Compare these separately:


1. HW3 assignment requirements provided above.
2. Week 3 readme.md.
3. Week 3 executable starter code.
4. Week 3 comments/TODO instructions.


Report every confirmed mismatch.


Check especially:


1. Top-5 recommendations versus single selected user/movie prediction.
2. User-only selector versus user + movie selector.
3. Missing-value strategy choices.
4. Any formula described in comments but not implemented.
5. Any behavior described in README but absent from code.
6. Any code structure that conflicts with the stated assignment.
7. Any README instruction that conflicts with the assignment-level wording.


Do not silently resolve any conflict in Step 1.




G. Inspect the repository-prescribed Top-5 behavior


Determine whether the local Week 3 README and starter code require:


1. One active user.
2. User-Based CF Top-5 recommendations.
3. Item-Based CF Top-5 recommendations.
4. Side-by-side comparison.
5. Predicted score or similarity displayed with each movie.
6. A default topK of 5.
7. A user-neighbor count such as N = 20.


Report exactly what is explicitly specified.


Do not assume a value is mandatory if it appears only as an example.




H. Dataset verification before editing


Using the actual local Week 3 files, report:


1. u.data file size.
2. u.item file size.
3. SHA-256 of u.data.
4. SHA-256 of u.item.
5. Number of rating rows.
6. Number of unique users.
7. Number of unique movies in ratings.
8. Number of parsed movies in u.item.
9. Minimum rating.
10. Maximum rating.
11. Minimum ratings per user.
12. Median ratings per user.
13. Maximum ratings per user.
14. Minimum ratings per movie.
15. Median ratings per movie.
16. Maximum ratings per movie.
17. Total possible user-item cells.
18. Number of observed ratings.
19. Sparsity percentage.


Use only the Week 3 local dataset files.


Do not copy or inspect dataset files from another homework folder.


Do not modify the datasets.




I. Build an initial hypothesis table


For each item classify it as:


CONFIRMED FROM CODE
NEEDS TESTING
NOT APPLICABLE YET


Check:


1. Rating matrix not implemented.
2. Rating matrix built incorrectly.
3. User-user similarity not implemented.
4. Item-item similarity not implemented.
5. Missing-value strategy not implemented.
6. Missing 0 values incorrectly treated as real ratings.
7. Zero denominator in similarity.
8. NaN similarity.
9. Infinity similarity.
10. Active user compared with itself.
11. Neighbors with no candidate-movie rating included incorrectly.
12. User-Based prediction denominator incorrect.
13. Item-Based prediction denominator incorrect.
14. User vectors built incorrectly.
15. Item vectors built incorrectly.
16. Very small overlap creates very high similarity.
17. Cold-start user cannot receive recommendations.
18. Cold-start item cannot be recommended.
19. Already-rated movies can appear as recommendations.
20. Duplicate recommendations can appear.
21. Recommendation score outside expected rating range.
22. Non-deterministic results for identical input.
23. User-Based and Item-Based logic accidentally use the same computation.
24. Expensive repeated full-matrix work.
25. UI or README behavior does not match the homework.




J. Plan User-Based CF before editing


Do not implement yet.


Explain:


1. What vector represents a user.
2. What co-rated movies means.
3. Which users should be compared with the active user.
4. Whether the active user should ever be compared with itself.
5. What a neighbor must have in order to contribute to a candidate movie.
6. What raw similarity formula the Week 3 materials support.
7. How missing ratings should be excluded or handled.
8. What prediction formula the repository supports.
9. How the denominator should be handled.
10. What happens when no valid neighbors exist.
11. How already-rated movies should be excluded.
12. How Top-5 should be selected.


If multiple formulas are possible, list them separately.


Do not silently choose one.




K. Plan Item-Based CF before editing


Do not implement yet.


Explain:


1. What vector represents a movie.
2. What common users means.
3. How two movie vectors should be compared.
4. Which movies rated by the active user contribute to a candidate.
5. What item-based prediction formula the Week 3 materials support.
6. How the denominator should be handled.
7. What happens when no similar rated items exist.
8. How already-rated movies should be excluded.
9. How Top-5 should be selected.


Do not implement yet.




L. Missing-value strategy analysis


The assignment asks to analyze:


1. Mean imputation.
2. Weighted by common ratings.
3. Matrix factorization.


The Week 3 repository may instead mention:


1. Co-rated only.
2. Mean imputation.
3. Weighted approach.


For each strategy that appears in the Week 3 materials or assignment requirements, report:


1. How it works.
2. Simplicity.
3. Bias risk.
4. Computational cost.
5. Suitability for MovieLens 100K.
6. Suitability for this vanilla JavaScript project.
7. Ease of testing.
8. Ease of explaining in the final report.
9. Whether it directly matches the assignment wording.
10. Whether it directly matches the Week 3 repository wording.


Clearly identify the mismatch between assignment-level options and repository options.


At the end give:


RECOMMENDATION ONLY — NOT IMPLEMENTED


Recommend which ONE strategy appears most defensible for HW3.


Do not implement it yet.




M. Check weighted-common-ratings formula


This is important.


Search all available Week 3 materials in the project for an exact weighted-common-ratings formula.


Report:


1. Whether an exact formula exists.
2. Exact source file or material.
3. Exact formula if present.
4. Whether a constant is specified.
5. Whether a cap is specified.
6. Whether the output is required to remain in [0,1].


Do not invent:


n / (n + 10)


or any other formula.


If the exact formula is absent, state:


WEIGHTING FORMULA UNDERSPECIFIED


Do not resolve it in Step 1.




N. Cold-start investigation


Using the actual Week 3 MovieLens data:


1. Determine whether every existing user has at least one rating.
2. Determine whether every existing movie has at least one rating.
3. Report the minimum rating count for users.
4. Report the minimum rating count for movies.
5. Explain why a true new user with zero ratings may have to be simulated.
6. Explain why a true new item with zero ratings may have to be simulated.
7. Propose a synthetic new-user test.
8. Propose a synthetic new-item test.


Do not implement synthetic entities yet.




O. Sparsity investigation


Using the real Week 3 dataset:


1. Find at least one user pair with zero common movies.
2. Find at least one user pair with exactly one or very few common movies.
3. Preferably find a pair with 2 to 4 common movies that is suitable for hand calculation.
4. Report:
   a. user IDs
   b. shared movie IDs
   c. shared movie titles if available
   d. ratings from both users
   e. common-count
   f. raw cosine similarity
5. If similarity is high despite very little overlap, explain that the concern is not that high similarity is automatically wrong; the concern is that it has little supporting evidence.
6. State exactly how the example was selected.




P. User-Based vs Item-Based efficiency plan


Let:


U = number of users
I = number of movies


Calculate:


User-user pair count:
U(U - 1) / 2


Item-item pair count:
I(I - 1) / 2


Report exact values from the Week 3 dataset.


Then explain:


1. Which pair space is larger for this dataset.
2. Why that matters computationally.
3. Why User-Based CF can become expensive when user count grows.
4. Why Item-Based CF can become expensive when item count grows.
5. Why neither approach should be described as universally faster.


Do not invent measured runtimes yet.




Q. Quality-comparison plan


The homework requires comparing recommendation quality.


Do not invent quality results.


Propose a fair evaluation plan for User-Based and Item-Based CF.


Consider:


1. Hold-one-out evaluation.
2. Train/test split.
3. MAE.
4. RMSE.
5. Coverage.
6. One controlled example.
7. Multiple known-rating prediction cases.


For each explain:


1. What it measures.
2. Whether it is practical for this assignment.
3. Whether it allows a fair comparison of both CF methods.
4. Whether it tests prediction accuracy or recommendation ranking quality.


Recommend one primary evaluation protocol for Step 3.


Do not execute the full evaluation yet.




R. Runtime-comparison plan


Do not invent runtime results.


Propose a reproducible runtime comparison between:


User-Based CF
Item-Based CF


Specify:


1. Same hardware/runtime environment.
2. Same selected users or evaluation set.
3. Same number of repeated runs.
4. Warm-up if necessary.
5. What timing function/tool to use.
6. Whether to report mean or median.
7. How to avoid including unrelated page-loading time.


Do not run the full benchmark yet unless needed only to understand the baseline.




S. Personal verification candidate


Choose one SMALL calculation that I can personally reproduce by hand later.


Prefer:


1. one user-user cosine similarity using 2 to 4 co-rated movies


or


2. one item-item cosine similarity using 2 to 4 common users


Give me:


1. Exact IDs.
2. Exact ratings.
3. Dot product.
4. Squared norms.
5. Formula.
6. Raw cosine result.
7. Common-count.


If weighted similarity is not yet fully specified, do not invent the weighted result.


Label it:


CANDIDATE FOR PERSONAL HAND VERIFICATION


Do NOT say that I personally verified it yet.




T. Plan implementation verification


For each major component propose:


1. Exact test.
2. Expected evidence.
3. What confirms correctness.
4. What would reveal a problem.


Include:


1. Rating matrix construction.
2. Known matrix cells.
3. Missing matrix cells.
4. User-user cosine.
5. Item-item cosine.
6. No common ratings.
7. Zero denominator.
8. Small overlap.
9. Weighted common-rating strategy.
10. User-Based recommendation score.
11. Item-Based recommendation score.
12. Already-rated candidate exclusion.
13. Top-5 count.
14. Descending sorting.
15. Duplicate recommendation check.
16. NaN check.
17. Infinity check.
18. Deterministic output.
19. Cold-start user.
20. Cold-start item.
21. Quality comparison.
22. Runtime comparison.




U. c1 and c2 evidence planning


For c1 identify:


1. Exact HW3 problem.
2. Exact implementation requirements.
3. Exact business-analysis requirements.
4. Week 3 source conflicts that must be handled carefully.
5. References that will later need verification.


For c2 identify:


1. Baseline evidence.
2. Functions that must be implemented.
3. Tests that must later be executed.
4. Personal hand-calculation candidate.
5. Cold-start evidence.
6. Sparsity evidence.
7. User-Based vs Item-Based quality evidence.
8. User-Based vs Item-Based efficiency evidence.
9. Missing-value strategy evidence.
10. Evidence that must be preserved in session.json.




V. Stop before editing


At the end return:


1. Baseline Summary
2. Week 3 Files Inspected
3. Confirmed Baseline Facts
4. Current Pipeline
5. TODO / Placeholder Functions
6. HW3 vs README vs Starter-Code Mismatches
7. Initial Hypothesis Table
8. Dataset Verification
9. User-Based CF Plan
10. Item-Based CF Plan
11. Missing-Value Strategy Analysis
12. Weighted Formula Status
13. Cold-Start Findings
14. Sparsity Findings
15. Efficiency Plan
16. Quality-Evaluation Plan
17. Runtime-Evaluation Plan
18. Candidate for Personal Hand Verification
19. Implementation Verification Plan
20. c1 Evidence Plan
21. c2 Evidence Plan
22. Files Likely to Need Modification in Step 2
23. Recommended Step 2


Then finish with:


AUDIT STATUS

Dataset modified: YES/NO
Implementation performed: YES/NO

parts.text:
# Step 1 — Baseline Audit Before Implementation

**The local project is a partially implemented Top-5 recommendation starter. Data loading, parsing, user selection, and list rendering exist; matrix construction, similarity, and both CF algorithms are unfinished.**

**No files were edited.** Before/after SHA-256 checks matched for all eight files in the Week 3 directory.

An important finding: **the lecture PDF does specify a weighted-common-ratings formula**, `final_sim = raw_sim × n / 50`. However, its uncapped result conflicts with the starter’s stated `[0,1]` similarity range. This remains unresolved.

## Evidence conventions

- **Code/material inspection:** directly supported by local source or lecture material.
- **Executed check:** actually run during this audit.
- **Proposed test/plan:** future work, not executed.
- **Conclusion:** interpretation of the stated evidence.

The audited directory was:

```text
/home/dastan/Recommender Systems/Week 3
```

The harness default working directory pointed elsewhere. All audit commands explicitly used the Week 3 directory. No previous-homework files were inspected or reused.

---

## 1. Baseline Summary

| Question | Finding |
|---|---|
| Does the project load and parse the local data? | **Yes in the executed JavaScript harness**, with qualifications below. Browser loading was not tested. |
| Does a rating matrix exist after loading? | **No.** `ratingMatrix` remains `null`. |
| Is cosine implemented? | **No.** It always returns `0`. |
| Does User-Based CF work? | **No.** Its function always returns `[]`. |
| Does Item-Based CF work? | **No.** Its function always returns `[]`. |
| Does the application currently generate Top-5 recommendations? | **No.** Both result lists are empty. |
| Does it instead predict one selected user/movie rating? | **No.** There is no movie selector or implemented single-rating predictor. |
| Is a missing-value strategy implemented? | **No.** All three strategy checkboxes remain unselected comments. |
| Is cold-start handling implemented? | **No algorithm-specific handling.** A generic empty-list message exists. |
| Does similarity account for overlap count? | **No.** Similarity ignores its inputs. |
| Were browser interactions verified? | **No.** |
| Was implementation performed? | **No.** |

**Executed-test boundary:** JavaScript ran using **Bun 1.4.2**, a VM context, mocked DOM elements, and a fetch adapter returning real local file bytes through `Response`. This tested executable application functions but did not test browser layout, browser networking, or actual clicks.

---

## 2. Week 3 Files Inspected

All eight local files were inspected or processed.

| File | Role and inspection |
|---|---|
| `index.html` | Page structure, user dropdown, recommendation button, two result sections, script loading order. Read completely. |
| `style.css` | Presentation, two-column result grid, one-column layout at widths ≤640px, control styling. Read completely. |
| `data.js` | Global data, fetching, parsers, dimension derivation, matrix TODO. Read completely and executed. |
| `script.js` | Initialization, dropdown, similarity/CF TODOs, recommendation dispatch, list renderer. Read completely and executed. |
| `readme.md` | Repository specification for two Top-5 lists and missing-value options. Read completely. |
| `LLM4RecSys 03. Collaborative Filtering.pptx.pdf` | All 22 pages inspected, including image-based formulas and screenshots. Important pages: 8–16 and 21. |
| `u.data` | Entire file processed for hashes, validation, statistics, and overlap examples; also parsed by the actual JavaScript parser. |
| `u.item` | Entire file processed for hashes, catalog validation, metadata, and encoding; also parsed by the actual JavaScript parser. |

The professor’s remote repository was **not needed for this audit**. No claim is made that the local files match the current remote revision.

### Data loading and parsing

**`u.item` — `data.js:19–27,52–69`**

1. `fetch('u.item')`.
2. Check `response.ok`; throw on failure.
3. Read using `response.text()`.
4. Split on newline; skip blank lines.
5. Split each line on `|`; skip lines with fewer than five fields.
6. Parse field 0 as movie ID; take field 1 as title.
7. Read genre flags with `fields.slice(5,24)`.
8. Push `{ id, title, genres }` into `movies`.

Release dates and URLs are not stored.

**`u.data` — `data.js:29–35,73–89`**

1. `fetch('u.data')`.
2. Check `response.ok`.
3. Read using `response.text()`.
4. Split on newline; skip blank lines.
5. Split on tabs; skip lines with fewer than four fields.
6. Parse `userId`, `itemId`, `rating`, and `timestamp`.
7. Push those four numeric fields into `ratings`.

### Current representations

- **Users:** numeric IDs in rating records; `numUsers` is the maximum ID. There are no separate user objects.
- **Movies:** objects in the `movies` array.
- **Ratings:** flat records in the `ratings` array.
- **Matrix:** a global initialized to `null`; construction is unfinished.
- **Missing ratings:** currently absent user/movie pairs in the flat records. `0` is the **documented future matrix sentinel**, not an existing matrix value.
- **Rated mask:** absent.

### Additional executed baseline findings

These were investigated and tested, rather than assumed:

1. **Genre mapping has a structural mismatch.**  
   The parser reads 19 flags but has only 18 genre names. The final flag is never mapped. Executing the parser produces:

   ```text
   Toy Story (1995) → ["Children's", "Comedy", "Crime"]
   ```

   Under the MovieLens genre layout, the first flag is `unknown`; the starter’s name list begins with `Action`, shifting the mapping. The executable 19-versus-18 mismatch is directly confirmed. Authoritative schema documentation should be cited before a later correction.

2. **UTF-8 text decoding damages some titles.**  
   Actual `Response.text()` decoding produced **12 replacement characters across nine movie titles**. For example:

   ```text
   Movie 543:
   Latin-1 decoding: Misérables, Les (1995)
   Response.text():  Mis�rables, Les (1995)
   ```

3. **Loading twice appends duplicate data.**  
   A second `loadData()` in the same context produced 3,364 movie objects and 200,000 rating objects; `numMovies` became 3,364. The standard initialization calls it once, so this is a confirmed reload issue, not evidence that the initial dataset contains duplicates.

4. **Load-error status is asymmetric.**  
   Simulated 404 responses for either dataset displayed an error in the User-Based section but left the Item-Based section at “Loading movie data...”.

None was corrected in Step 1.

---

## 3. Confirmed Baseline Facts

| Fact | Result | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Users | **943** | Full dataset scan and actual JS loading |
| Catalog movies | **1,682** | Full catalog scan and actual JS parsing |
| Ratings | **100,000** | Full scan and actual JS parsing |
| Rating scale | Integers `{1,2,3,4,5}` | Full scan |
| Minimum / maximum rating | **1 / 5** | Full scan |
| User IDs | Contiguous **1–943**, 1-based | Full scan |
| Movie IDs | Contiguous **1–1682**, 1-based | Full scan |
| Is `0` an observed rating? | **No** | Full scan |
| Does `0` mean “not rated”? | **Specified convention only**; matrix absent | Code/comments |
| `buildRatingMatrix()` | Empty function; returns `undefined`; matrix remains `null` | Code and execution |
| `cosineSimilarity()` | Constant `0` | Code and six executed fixtures |
| User-Based CF | Unimplemented | Every existing user tested |
| Item-Based CF | Unimplemented | Every existing user tested |
| Actual Top-5 output | None | Both methods return `[]` |
| Single selected-rating output | Absent | HTML/function inspection |
| Missing values | Untreated algorithmically | No implemented matrix/similarity |
| Cold-start handling | Absent | No history/zero-column logic |
| Co-rated-count handling | Absent | No overlap computation |
| Identical-input determinism | Confirmed for current empty outputs | Two calls per method per existing user |

### NaN and Infinity: precise distinction

- Current cosine returns finite `0`.
- Current recommendation functions produce **no scores**, so they do not presently generate `NaN` or `Infinity`.
- No prediction division exists yet.
- **Executed renderer test:** externally supplied `NaN` and `Infinity` scores are rendered literally. `renderList()` has no finite-number validation.

Thus, “prediction scores currently become NaN” is **not confirmed**. “The renderer accepts nonfinite fixture scores” **is confirmed**.

### What the UI currently contains

- One active-user dropdown.
- One **Get Recommendations** button.
- Separate User-Based and Item-Based result sections.
- No movie selector.
- No strategy selector.
- No neighbor-count control.
- No Top-K control.
- No single-rating prediction control.

The harness populated **943 user options plus one placeholder**. An empty selection produced “Please select a user first.” Selecting user 1 produced the TODO empty-list message in both sections.

---

## 4. Current Pipeline

| Stage | Actual baseline behavior |
|---|---|
| 1. Data loading | `window.onload()` awaits `loadData()`; `u.item` is requested before `u.data`. |
| 2. Data parsing | Both parsers populate flat arrays. |
| 3. Matrix construction | Dimensions are assigned, then **`buildRatingMatrix()` does nothing**. This is the first missing computational stage. |
| 4. User selection | Initialization continues, populates the dropdown, and announces “Data loaded.” |
| 5. Similarity calculation | Not reached through the recommendation functions. Direct cosine calls return `0`. |
| 6. Neighbor / similar-item selection | Absent in both CF functions. |
| 7. Prediction calculation | Absent. |
| 8. Candidate filtering | Absent. |
| 9. Sorting/ranking | Absent. |
| 10. Top-K selection | Default parameter exists; selection logic does not. |
| 11. UI rendering | `getRecommendations()` passes two empty arrays to `renderList()`, which renders the TODO message. |

**Important:** the computational pipeline is incomplete at `buildRatingMatrix()`, but JavaScript control flow does not halt there. Its no-op return allows initialization and the empty recommendation UI to continue.

---

## 5. TODO / Placeholder Functions

| Function | Location | Current placeholder |
|---|---|---|
| `buildRatingMatrix()` | `data.js:104–106` | Empty body; implicit `undefined`; leaves global matrix `null`. |
| `cosineSimilarity(a,b)` | `script.js:62–65` | `return 0`. |
| `getUserBasedRecommendations(activeUserId, topK=5)` | `script.js:80–83` | `return []`. |
| `getItemBasedRecommendations(activeUserId, topK=5)` | `script.js:98–101` | `return []`. |

No unfinished function explicitly returns `null`; `null` is the matrix’s initial state.

The implemented functions are `loadData`, both parsers, initialization, `populateUserDropdown`, `getRecommendations`, and `renderList`. Their existence does not establish an operational recommender.

---

## 6. HW3 vs README vs Starter-Code Mismatches

### Sources considered separately

1. **Your assignment requirements:** both CF methods; one of mean imputation, common-rating weighting, or matrix factorization; quality, efficiency, strategy trade-offs, cold-start and sparsity analysis.
2. **Local README:** user-only, side-by-side Top-5 workflow; cosine; co-rated-only, mean imputation, or weighting.
3. **Executable starter:** the requested UI shell, with four unfinished computational functions.
4. **Starter comments/TODOs:** co-rated cosine, `[0,1]`, positive user neighbors, weighted-average User-Based prediction, item aggregation.
5. **Local lecture PDF:** additional formulas, signed/centered examples, a weighting constant, and a single-rating UI illustration.

### Confirmed differences and omissions

| Topic | Evidence and status |
|---|---|
| **Top-5 vs single-rating UI** | README §§1–2,5 and local HTML specify two lists for one user. PDF p.21 illustrates a selected user **and movie**, a “Predict Rating” button, and two scalar predictions. **Confirmed material discrepancy.** |
| **User-only vs user+movie selector** | Local executable HTML has only `user-select`; PDF p.21 has both selectors. |
| **Assignment strategy choices** | Assignment and PDF p.21: mean, weighting, factorization. README §6 and starter header: co-rated-only, mean, weighting. Co-rated-only is an extra repository option; factorization is omitted there. |
| **Lecture itself has different option lists** | PDF p.16 follows the README’s three choices; p.21 uses the assignment’s three choices. |
| **Mean imputation vs co-rated-only wording** | README §5.3 and cosine TODO say to compare only co-rated entries, while README §6 permits mean imputation. A literal co-rated-only calculation would not use filled missing entries. |
| **Weighted formula range** | PDF p.16 gives `raw_sim × n/50`; `script.js:60` requires `[0,1]`. No cap is supplied. Real-data counterexample confirms incompatibility. |
| **Similarity family** | README/starter focus on nonnegative raw cosine. PDF pp.7–9,11 discusses Pearson, adjusted cosine, and negative similarities. These are distinct variants, not implemented equivalents. |
| **User prediction formula** | README/TODO describe an average of raw ratings weighted by positive similarity. PDF p.9 illustrates a user baseline plus weighted neighbor deviations, including negative similarities. |
| **Item prediction formula** | README/TODO say “aggregate” similarity-weighted user ratings, without an explicit denominator. PDF p.11 illustrates an item baseline plus weighted item-mean deviations. |
| **Matrix orientation** | PDF pp.12,21 describes users as columns and items as rows. Starter uses `ratingMatrix[userId][movieId]`: users are rows. This is a transpose convention, **not inherently an algorithmic error**. |
| **Specified algorithms vs executable code** | Matrix, cosine, neighbor selection, predictions, candidate exclusion, sorting, and Top-K are specified but absent. These are explicit starter TODOs. |
| **Display explanation text** | README §5.6 asks for “Because you...” explanations. The current renderer emits a plain list, or the TODO message. |
| **Top-5 instruction text** | README §2 requests an instruction mentioning two Top-5 lists; the HTML says “two ways” without stating Top-5. |
| **Graceful insufficient-history message** | README requests a clear empty case; current text says to implement the TODO, without distinguishing cold start or insufficient support. |
| **Genre field/name count** | README asks for 18 names while reading 19 flags. Starter follows that inconsistent mapping; the executed parser confirms its consequence. |
| **Offline/static hosting wording** | README §7 combines “offline”, `file://`-like hosting, and GitHub Pages. GitHub Pages uses HTTPS; local `file://` fetch behavior is browser-dependent/restricted. Browser behavior here remains untested. |
| **Business analysis coverage** | The assignment requires quality, efficiency and trade-off evidence. No local report or evaluation code exists. This is an unmet deliverable, not a contradictory formula. |

The PDF contains earlier-exercise recap slides. They were identified as recap material and were not used as implementation requirements.

### Exactly what the local repository prescribes for Top-5

| Requirement | Explicit? |
|---|---|
| One active user | **Yes** |
| User-Based Top-5 | **Yes** |
| Item-Based Top-5 | **Yes** |
| Side-by-side comparison | **Yes**; CSS also specifies stacking on narrow screens |
| Title plus predicted score or similarity | **Yes**, README §2 |
| Default `topK=5` | **Yes**, README and both function signatures |
| User-neighbor selection | **Yes**, top positive-similarity neighbors |
| Mandatory `N=20` | **No**. It is explicitly an example: “e.g., N = 20”. |
| Single selected movie prediction | **Not in the local README/HTML workflow**; shown in PDF p.21 |

No conflict has been resolved in this audit.

---

## 7. Initial Hypothesis Table

“NOT APPLICABLE YET” means the relevant algorithmic operation does not exist; it does not certify the future implementation.

| # | Hypothesis | Classification | Evidence / conclusion |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rating matrix not implemented | **CONFIRMED FROM CODE** | Empty body; execution leaves `null`. |
| 2 | Rating matrix built incorrectly | **NOT APPLICABLE YET** | No matrix is built. |
| 3 | User-user similarity not implemented | **CONFIRMED FROM CODE** | Shared cosine stub; no user comparison loop. |
| 4 | Item-item similarity not implemented | **CONFIRMED FROM CODE** | No column comparisons. |
| 5 | Missing-value strategy not implemented | **CONFIRMED FROM CODE** | Header choices unselected; no calculation. |
| 6 | Missing zeros treated as real ratings | **NOT APPLICABLE YET** | No matrix calculation. |
| 7 | Zero denominator in similarity | **NOT APPLICABLE YET** | No denominator exists. Zero-vector fixture returns constant `0`. |
| 8 | NaN similarity | **NOT APPLICABLE YET** | Stub always returns finite `0`. |
| 9 | Infinity similarity | **NOT APPLICABLE YET** | Same. |
| 10 | Active user compared with itself | **NOT APPLICABLE YET** | No comparison loop. |
| 11 | Neighbors without candidate ratings included | **NOT APPLICABLE YET** | No neighbor aggregation. |
| 12 | User-Based denominator incorrect | **NOT APPLICABLE YET** | No prediction formula. |
| 13 | Item-Based denominator incorrect | **NOT APPLICABLE YET** | No prediction formula; specification also needs clarification. |
| 14 | User vectors built incorrectly | **NOT APPLICABLE YET** | No vectors built. |
| 15 | Item vectors built incorrectly | **NOT APPLICABLE YET** | No vectors built. |
| 16 | Small overlap creates high similarity | **NEEDS TESTING** in the app | Independent dataset arithmetic confirms the phenomenon; application cosine remains a stub. |

## 9. User-Based CF Plan

**Proposed only.**

### Representation and comparisons

- User \(u\) is represented by row \(R[u][1..I]\).
- Co-rated movies are movies with observed ratings from both users:
  \[
  C_{uv}=\{i:R_{ui}>0\land R_{vi}>0\}.
  \]
- Compare the active user with every **other** eligible user.
- Exclude the active user from recommendation-neighbor selection. Self-similarity may be a unit-test fixture, but not a contributing neighbor.

### Raw similarity supported by the repository

\[
s_{\mathrm{raw}}(u,v)=
\frac{\sum_{i\in C_{uv}}R_{ui}R_{vi}}
{\sqrt{\sum_{i\in C_{uv}}R_{ui}^{2}}
 \sqrt{\sum_{i\in C_{uv}}R_{vi}^{2}}}.
\]

For co-rated/weighted handling, missing entries do not enter these sums. A mean-imputation choice would require a separately documented calculation domain and observation mask.

No overlap or zero norm must produce the documented guarded value `0`.

### Neighbor selection

The README suggests selecting the global top \(N\) positive-similarity users first. For candidate movie \(j\), only selected neighbors who **actually rated \(j\)** may contribute:

\[
N_j(u)=\{v\in N(u):R_{vj}>0\}.
\]

A per-candidate top-\(N\) selection is another possible design, but it is not the README’s stated sequence and must not be substituted silently.

### Prediction formulas must remain distinct

**A. Repository-supported raw weighted average**

\[
\hat R_{uj}=
\frac{\sum_{v\in N_j(u)}s(u,v)R_{vj}}
{\sum_{v\in N_j(u)}s(u,v)}.
\]

Only contributors belong in both numerator and denominator. With positive weights, this stays within the contributing ratings’ range.

**B. Lecture-supported centered variant — PDF p.9**

The slide’s baseline-plus-deviation example corresponds to:

\[
\hat R_{uj}=
\bar R_u+
\frac{\sum_v s(u,v)(R_{vj}-\bar R_v)}
{\sum_v |s(u,v)|}.
\]

It supports signed similarities and differs from A. Exact mean populations and neighbor rules would need documentation before adoption.

### Unsupported candidates and Top-5

Recommended behavior, subject to Step 2 approval:

- If the contributor set is empty or denominator is zero, mark the candidate unsupported and omit it.
- Do not fabricate a rating of zero.
- Exclude all movies already rated by the active user using observed ratings.
- Sort supported candidates by score descending.
- Use movie ID ascending for deterministic ties.
- Take at most five.
- If fewer than five candidates are supported, show fewer with an explanatory message.

No choice between prediction variants has been implemented.

## 10. Item-Based CF Plan

**Proposed only.**

- Movie \(i\) is represented by column \(R[1..U][i]\).
- Common users are users who rated both movies:
  \[
  C_{ij}=\{u:R_{ui}>0\land R_{uj}>0\}.
  \]
- Apply the selected similarity convention consistently to the two item vectors.
- For an unrated candidate \(j\), only movies actually rated by the active user contribute.
- No “liked means ≥4” threshold is specified; the README says **rated** movies.

### Possible formulas

**A. Normalized raw weighted average**

A natural explicit interpretation of similarity-weighted aggregation is:

\[
\hat R_{uj}=
\frac{\sum_{i\in H_u}s(j,i)R_{ui}}
{\sum_{i\in H_u}s(j,i)},
\]

using eligible positive-similarity items from the user’s observed history \(H_u\).

**B. Unnormalized aggregation**

The README’s word “aggregate” could also be read as:

\[
\operatorname{score}(u,j)=\sum_{i\in H_u}s(j,i)R_{ui}.
\]

That is a ranking score, not necessarily a rating prediction in `[1,5]`. The README does not explicitly settle the denominator.

**C. Lecture’s item-baseline variant — PDF p.11**

The example corresponds to:

\[
\hat R_{uj}=
\bar R_j+
\frac{\sum_{i\in H_u}s(j,i)(R_{ui}-\bar R_i)}
{\sum_{i\in H_u}|s(j,i)|}.
\]

This is distinct from A and B.

For a normalized approach, no contributors/zero denominator should yield an unsupported candidate, not a division. Candidate exclusion, deterministic descending sorting, uniqueness, and at-most-five selection should follow the same policy as User-Based CF.

## 11. Missing-Value Strategy Analysis

These are conceptual trade-offs, not measured quality results.

| Strategy | How it works | Simplicity and bias | Computational cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Co-rated only** | Calculate similarity using jointly observed coordinates. | Simplest. Avoids fabricated ratings, but very small overlaps can dominate and observation patterns are selective. | Dense scan \(O(d)\) per pair; sparse intersections can reduce work. |
| **Mean imputation** | Fill missing coordinates using a specified user/item mean before similarity. | Relatively simple. Shrinks variation and can create artificial similarity; empty-history means are undefined without a policy. | Means \(O(M)\); full materialization \(O(UI)\); dense comparisons typically \(O(d)\). |
| **Weighted common ratings** | Compute raw similarity and scale by overlap support. PDF gives \(n/50\). | Modest complexity. Addresses weak support, but can favor prolific users/popular items; uncapped scaling changes score magnitude. | Overlap count can be accumulated during similarity, adding little asymptotic cost. |
| **Matrix factorization** | Fit user/item latent factors to observed ratings; infer missing scores. | Most complex. Regularization/rank choices matter; popularity and observation bias remain possible. | Typical training roughly \(O(E M f)\), with epochs \(E\), observed ratings \(M\), factors \(f\). Additional work if used to fill a matrix for memory-based CF. |

Here \(d\) is the comparison-vector length.

### Fit, testing, explanation, and wording

| Strategy | MovieLens 100K suitability | Vanilla JS suitability | Testing / explaining | Assignment wording | Local README wording |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Co-rated only | Useful baseline, but sparse evidence is a major concern | Excellent | Easy numerical fixtures and explanation | **Not explicitly listed** as the selected strategy | **Direct match** |
| Mean imputation | Feasible; high sparsity makes artificial evidence important | Good | Easy fixtures; mean direction and mask must be explicit | **Direct match** | **Direct match** |
| Weighted common ratings | Strong conceptual fit for the stated sparsity analysis | Good | Easy once formula/range contract is settled; clear explanation of evidence support | **Direct match** | **Direct match** |
| Matrix factorization | Feasible for this dataset, but needs tuning and evaluation | Possible, substantially more engineering | Harder: training convergence, seed, rank, regularization and leakage checks | **Direct match** | **Not listed in §6**; discussed in PDF |

The PDF also mentions KNN as an advanced technique on p.13. It is a neighbor-selection/model family, not by itself a completely specified missing-value policy.

### RECOMMENDATION ONLY — NOT IMPLEMENTED

**Recommend weighted common-rating handling**, conditional on resolving the lecture formula’s range conflict before implementation.

Reasons:

- It directly matches both assignment and README wording.
- It addresses the assignment’s low-overlap reliability concern.
- It fits the existing cosine/neighbor starter.
- The lecture supplies an actual formula and constant.
- Its arithmetic is straightforward to test and explain.

This recommendation does **not** approve a cap, replace `50`, or choose a different weighting formula.

## 15. Efficiency Plan

Using the actual dataset dimensions:

\[
\text{User pairs}
=\frac{943(943-1)}2
=\boxed{444153}
\]

\[
\text{Item pairs}
=\frac{1682(1682-1)}2
=\boxed{1413721}
\]

The item-pair space is approximately **3.18 times larger**.

### Computational implications

- An exhaustive user-user cache has fewer distinct pairs here.
- Each dense user comparison scans **1,682 movie coordinates**.
- Each dense item comparison scans **943 user coordinates**.
- Dense all-pairs costs are approximately:
  - User-Based: \(O(U^2I)\)
  - Item-Based: \(O(I^2U)\)
- Sparse intersections, caching, neighborhood limits, and query patterns change actual cost.
- User-Based pair storage/computation grows quadratically with users.
- Item-Based pair storage/computation grows quadratically with items.
- A per-user query need not calculate every pair in either space.

**Conclusion:** pair counts motivate an efficiency hypothesis; they are not measured runtimes. Neither method is universally faster.

### Recommended primary protocol for Step 3

4. Predict the **same 943 targets** using both methods.
5. Report:

parts.text:
# Step 2 — Implementation and Implementation-Level Verification

**Both CF methods are implemented and produced Top-5 recommendations in executable tests and a real Chrome browser.** The application retains one user selector and two side-by-side recommendation lists.

**All 34 implementation test groups passed.** `u.data`, `u.item`, and `readme.md` retain their original SHA-256 hashes.

**Important observed result:** baseline/deviation predictions can exceed 5. These scores were **not clipped**. Examples and their exact values appear below.

---

## 1. Implementation Summary

Implemented:

- Raw-ID user–item rating matrix.
- Observed-only user and item means.
- Separately testable raw cosine, overlap count, support weight, and weighted similarity.
- Capped common-rating weighting:
  ```js
  rawCosine * Math.min(commonCount / 50, 1)
  ```
- User-Based prediction using the active-user baseline and neighbor rating deviations.
- Item-Based prediction using the target-item baseline and rated-item deviations.
- Top-20 positive-similarity user neighbors.
- Unrated-candidate filtering, finite-score validation, deterministic ranking, and Top-5 selection.
- Loading, ready, calculating, no-evidence, and error UI states.
- Reproducible component and real-browser verification scripts.

No full quality evaluation, runtime benchmark, business analysis, or final report was produced.

---

## 2. Baseline Reconfirmation

Before editing, all eight requested starter characteristics were confirmed:

| Baseline characteristic | Confirmed |
|---|---|
| Unfinished `buildRatingMatrix()` | Yes |
| `cosineSimilarity()` returned `0` | Yes |
| User-Based function returned `[]` | Yes |
| Item-Based function returned `[]` | Yes |
| One user dropdown | Yes |
| Get Recommendations button | Yes |
| User-Based output area | Yes |
| Item-Based output area | Yes |

All seven source/dataset hashes matched Step 1.

**Directory change reported before editing:** the lecture PDF was no longer present. Formula references used the lecture pages already inspected during Step 1 in this conversation, together with your explicit Step 2 instructions. I did not restore or replace the PDF.

---

## 3. Files Changed

### Existing files modified

| File | Changes |
|---|---|
| `data.js` | Matrix, observed-rating indexes, means, reload handling, title decoding, genre alignment |
| `script.js` | Similarity, weighting, both CF methods, prediction arithmetic, caching, ranking, UI states |
| `index.html` | Clarified Top-5 instructions, active-user label, status area, loading-state controls |
| `style.css` | Ranked-list presentation, predicted-rating styling, status and disabled-control styling |

### Verification files added

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `verification.test.js` | Reproducible component, fixture, lecture, real-data, cold-start, and integrity checks |
| `browser-verification.js` | Real Chrome verification through the browser’s DevTools Protocol |

### Protected files unchanged

- `u.data`
- `u.item`
- `readme.md`

The temporary Chrome profile was created inside the Week 3 directory and removed after verification.

---

## 4. Rating Matrix Implementation

Implemented in `data.js:102`.

```js
ratingMatrix[userId][movieId]
```

Properties:

- Shape: **944 × 1683**, including reserved index-zero row and column.
- Every cell starts at `0`.
- All 100,000 observed ratings are inserted by raw ID.
- Missing cells remain `0`.
- Observed ratings are validated as integers from 1 through 5.
- Duplicate user/movie records are rejected.
- Rows are independent arrays.

Supporting structures remain in `data.js`:

- `moviesById`
- `ratedMovieIds`
- `itemRaterIds`
- Cached `userMeans` and `itemMeans`
- `getUserMean(userId)`
- `getItemMean(movieId)`

Means exclude missing cells. A user/item without observations has baseline **`null`**, rather than a fabricated zero rating.

**TEST RESULT:** every source rating matched its matrix cell; every matrix value was finite and either zero or a valid 1–5 rating.

---

## 5. Raw Cosine Implementation

Implemented through:

- `getCosineDetails(a, b)`
- `rawCosineSimilarity(a, b)`
- `cosineSimilarity(a, b)` — returns the weighted result
- `getItemCosineDetails(movieA, movieB)`

Only jointly observed coordinates enter the calculation:

\[
C=\{k:a_k\ne0\land b_k\ne0\}
\]

\[
s_{\text{raw}}=
\frac{\sum_{k\in C}a_kb_k}
{\sqrt{\sum_{k\in C}a_k^2}\sqrt{\sum_{k\in C}b_k^2}}.
\]

`getCosineDetails()` exposes:

```text
dot
squaredNormA
squaredNormB
commonCount
rawCosine
supportWeight
weightedSimilarity
```

Zero overlap or zero denominator produces `0`. Invalid/nonfinite input vectors are rejected. A floating-point boundary guard keeps raw positive-rating cosine within `[0,1]`; this is **not prediction clipping**.

Item comparisons use sparse common-user traversal. Tests compared this implementation against dense matrix-column calculations.

---

## 6. Common-Rating Weighting

### SOURCE-DERIVED FORMULA

Lecture page 16:

\[
s_{\text{final}}=s_{\text{raw}}\frac{n}{50}.
\]

### IMPLEMENTATION DECISION — explicitly approved in Step 2

\[
w(n)=\min\left(\frac n{50},1\right)
\]

\[
s_{\text{weighted}}=s_{\text{raw}}w(n).
\]

The lecture supplied **50**. Your implementation instructions supplied the **cap**.

| Common count | Tested support weight |
|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.02 |
| 3 | 0.06 |
| 40 | 0.80 |
| 50 | 1.00 |
| 80 | 1.00 |

**TEST RESULT:** weighted similarity stayed in `[0,1]` and did not exceed raw cosine in all weighting fixtures.

No alternative weighting formula, mean imputation, or factorization was introduced.

---

## 7. User-Based Prediction Formula

### SOURCE-DERIVED FORMULA

The lecture page 9 example supplies the structure:

\[
\boxed{
\hat r_{ui}
=
\bar r_u+
\frac{
\sum_{v\in N_i(u)}
s(u,v)(r_{vi}-\bar r_v)
}{
\sum_{v\in N_i(u)}|s(u,v)|
}
}
\]

Where:

- **Baseline:** active user’s observed-rating mean, \(\bar r_u\).
- **Deviation:** neighbor’s candidate rating minus that neighbor’s mean.
- **Contribution:** weighted user similarity multiplied by the deviation.
- **Denominator:** sum of absolute similarities of contributing neighbors.

### IMPLEMENTATION DECISIONS

- User means use **all observed ratings for that user**, not only pairwise overlap.
- Select the top **20** positive-similarity neighbors globally.
- Exclude the active user before similarity calculation.
- For each candidate, only selected neighbors who rated it contribute.
- No contributing evidence/zero denominator → `null`, and the candidate is excluded.
- No prediction clipping.

The lecture’s approximate displayed calculation was also tested:

\[
4.33-\frac{3.667}{2.866}
=3.050516399\ldots
\approx3.05.
\]

The test distinguishes illustrative values from hidden exact slide decimals.

---

## 8. Item-Based Prediction Formula

### SOURCE-DERIVED FORMULA

Lecture page 11 and your explicit Step 2 equation:

\[
\boxed{
\hat r_{ui}
=
\bar r_i+
\frac{
\sum_{j\in H_u}
s(i,j)(r_{uj}-\bar r_j)
}{
\sum_{j\in H_u}|s(i,j)|
}
}
\]

Where:

- \(\bar r_i\): **target candidate item’s** mean across observed ratings.
- \(H_u\): items already rated by the active user.
- \(\bar r_j\): observed mean of rated comparison item \(j\).
- \(r_{uj}-\bar r_j\): active user’s deviation from that item’s mean.
- Numerator preserves similarity signs.
- Denominator uses absolute similarities.

Missing zeros never enter item means.

The implementation does **not** use a weighted average of raw user ratings as the final Item-Based prediction formula.

**Important distinction:** runtime similarity is raw cosine over positive ratings, so its values are nonnegative. Signed lecture fixtures separately verify that the prediction equation preserves signs and uses the absolute denominator.

---

## 9. Lecture 2.58 Verification

### TEST RESULT — slide aggregate values

\[
3.67+\frac{-2.764}{2.543}
=
\boxed{2.583094769956744}
\]

Rounded to two decimals:

\[
\boxed{2.58}
\]

### TEST RESULT — displayed rounded component values

Using the implementation’s prediction helper:

\[
3.67+
\frac{
-0.99(5-3.33)
+0.72(3-3.00)
-0.84(5-3.67)
}{
0.99+0.72+0.84
}
\]

produced:

\[
\boxed{2.5835294117647054}
\approx2.58.
\]

These two values differ slightly because the displayed similarities and inferred means are rounded. The tests **do not claim to recover every hidden decimal**.

These are lecture fixtures, not MovieLens runtime observations. No overlap counts or support weights were invented for them.

---

## 10. User-Based CF Implementation

The implemented sequence is:

1. Validate the active user and observed baseline.
2. Compare its rating row with every other eligible user.
3. Compute co-rated raw cosine and capped support weighting.
4. Retain positive similarities.
5. Sort by similarity descending, then user ID ascending.
6. Keep at most 20 neighbors.
7. Visit unrated catalog movies.
8. Aggregate only neighbors who rated each candidate.
9. Apply the lecture baseline/deviation equation.
10. Exclude unsupported/nonfinite results.
11. Sort by full-precision score descending, then movie ID ascending.
12. Return up to five objects:

```js
{ movieId, title, score }
```

The existing UI remains recommendation-based; the internal prediction helper does not add a single-rating interface.

---

## 11. Item-Based CF Implementation

The implemented sequence is:

1. Validate the active user and rating history.
2. Visit unrated catalog movies.
3. Require an observed target-item mean.
4. Compare the target item against items already rated by the user.
5. Compute similarity through **common users**, not common movies.
6. Apply the same support weighting.
7. Aggregate rated-item deviations around their respective item means.
8. Add the target-item baseline.
9. Exclude zero-denominator/nonfinite predictions.
10. Sort deterministically and return Top-5.

Item-pair similarities are cached symmetrically. Rebuilding the rating matrix invalidates that cache.

**The methods remain distinct:** User-Based uses neighboring **users**; Item-Based uses the active user’s rated **items**. They share only the mathematical baseline/deviation aggregation helper.

---

## 12. UI / UX Changes

Preserved:

- Main heading: **Collaborative Filtering Movie Recommender**
- One user dropdown.
- Get Recommendations button.
- User-Based and Item-Based cards.
- Side-by-side desktop layout.

Added or improved:

- Explicit explanation of two Top-5 lists for the same user.
- Active-user label.
- Ranked ordered lists.
- Movie titles and **Predicted rating: X.XXX**.
- Loading, ready, calculating, no-evidence, and error messages.
- Disabled controls during loading/calculation.
- Accessible status and busy indicators.
- Both cards receive loading errors.
- Safe text rendering for movie titles.
- Visible explanation when returned estimates fall outside 1–5.

No movie selector, strategy selector, extra page, or chart was added.

Related tested loading fixes:

- Correct accented movie titles through Latin-1 decoding.
- Correct genre alignment after the `unknown` flag.
- Reloading replaces arrays instead of duplicating data.

---

## 13. Executable Tests

Run from:

```text
/home/dastan/Recommender Systems/Week 3
```

### Component and integration checks

```sh
bun verification.test.js
```

### Real-browser verification

```sh
bun browser-verification.js
```

Both use runtime/browser built-ins without external packages.

The first component-test run exposed a **test-harness injection problem**: an external assignment did not replace the VM’s similarity binding. The isolated signed-similarity fixture was corrected to assign within the VM context. The subsequent complete run passed.

No production formula was changed to accommodate that test failure.

---

## 14. Exact Test Results

### Overall result

**34 implementation test groups passed.**

| Area | Executed result |
|---|---|
| Dataset counts | 943 users, 1,682 movies, 100,000 ratings |
| Matrix shape | 944 × 1683 |
| Known cells | `R[196][242]=3`; `R[1][1]=5` |
| Missing cell | `R[1][273]=0` |
| Matrix integrity | All source records matched; 100,000 observed cells |
| Numeric matrix validity | All finite; nonzero entries are integers 1–5 |

80: // Parse rating data from u.data format
81: function parseRatingData(text) {
82:     const lines = text.split('\n');
83: 
84:     for (const line of lines) {
85:         if (line.trim() === '') continue;
86: 
87:         const fields = line.split('\t');
88:         if (fields.length < 4) continue; // Skip invalid lines
89: 
90:         const userId = parseInt(fields[0]);
91:         const itemId = parseInt(fields[1]);
92:         const rating = parseFloat(fields[2]);
93:         const timestamp = parseInt(fields[3]);
94: 
95:         ratings.push({ userId, itemId, rating, timestamp });
96:     }
97: }
98: 
99: // Raw-ID matrix; row/column 0 are reserved. Missing cells stay 0, never imputed.
100: // Means use observed ratings only. Sparse ID indexes support column comparisons
101: // without repeatedly scanning every user. Rebuilding replaces all derived data.
102: function buildRatingMatrix() {
103:     ratingMatrix = Array.from({ length: numUsers + 1 }, () => Array(numMovies + 1).fill(0));
104:     moviesById = new Map(movies.map(movie => [movie.id, movie]));
105:     ratedMovieIds = Array.from({ length: numUsers + 1 }, () => []);
106:     itemRaterIds = Array.from({ length: numMovies + 1 }, () => []);
107:     userMeans = Array(numUsers + 1).fill(null);
108:     itemMeans = Array(numMovies + 1).fill(null);
109:     const userSums = Array(numUsers + 1).fill(0);
110:     const itemSums = Array(numMovies + 1).fill(0);
111: 
112:     for (const { userId, itemId, rating } of ratings) {
113:         if (!Number.isInteger(userId) || userId < 1 || userId > numUsers ||
114:             !Number.isInteger(itemId) || itemId < 1 || itemId > numMovies ||
115:             !moviesById.has(itemId) || !Number.isInteger(rating) || rating < 1 || rating > 5) {
116:             throw new Error('Invalid user, movie, or rating in the dataset.');
117:         }
118:         if (ratingMatrix[userId][itemId] !== 0) {
119:             throw new Error(`Duplicate rating for user ${userId}, movie ${itemId}.`);
120:         }
121:         ratingMatrix[userId][itemId] = rating;
122:         ratedMovieIds[userId].push(itemId);
123:         itemRaterIds[itemId].push(userId);
124:         userSums[userId] += rating;
125:         itemSums[itemId] += rating;
126:     }
127: 
128:     for (let userId = 1; userId <= numUsers; userId++) {
129:         ratedMovieIds[userId].sort((a, b) => a - b);
130:         if (ratedMovieIds[userId].length) {
131:             userMeans[userId] = userSums[userId] / ratedMovieIds[userId].length;
132:         }
133:     }
134:     for (let movieId = 1; movieId <= numMovies; movieId++) {
135:         itemRaterIds[movieId].sort((a, b) => a - b);
136:         if (itemRaterIds[movieId].length) {
137:             itemMeans[movieId] = itemSums[movieId] / itemRaterIds[movieId].length;
138:         }
139:     }
140: }
141: 
142: // null means no observed baseline; it is not a fabricated zero rating.
143: function getItemMean(movieId) {
144:     return itemMeans[movieId] ?? null;
145: }
146: 
147: function getUserMean(userId) {
148:     return userMeans[userId] ?? null;
149: }

parts.text: **Preparing evaluation script**
**Predeclaring evaluation protocol**

The Step 2 production hashes and all ten specified algorithm/UI properties are unchanged. The lecture PDF is present again, and I rechecked its relevant pages.

I’ll use these fixed choices:
- **943 held-out cases:** one per user, selecting the latest timestamp; ties use the lowest movie ID. Each case starts from the full dataset minus that one rating.
- **Training-history bins:** 19–49, 50–99, 100–199, and 200+; 19 accounts for hiding one rating from a 20-rating user.
- **Overlap analysis:** all user pairs and all item pairs.
- **Runtime sample:** 20 users, five spread across each history-size bin; Top-5, two untimed warm-ups, five measured repeats, with separate cold- and warm-cache scenarios.

parts.text:
All hashes match the recorded Step 2 values. All evidence saved and validated.

Now report concisely. The user's constraint: don't declare a winner, don't draft the report. Present the evidence findings. Keep it reasonably concise but this is substantial evidence — a compact summary table is appropriate. The instruction says keep under 4 lines unless detail needed; but this is a results report where the user asked for evidence. I'll give a moderately compact summary.

Key numbers:

Quality (943 held-out, latest per user):
- User-based: coverage 94.59% (892/943), MAE 0.831, RMSE 1.081
- Item-based: coverage 99.79% (941/943), MAE 0.807, RMSE 1.036
- Common 892 pairs: User MAE 0.831/RMSE 1.081; Item MAE 0.794/RMSE 1.021
- By history bin, item-based coverage ≥99.3% everywhere, user-based degrades 99.7% → 79.1% as history grows (neighbors with 20-item cap can't always cover heavily-rated users)
- Out of range: User 28/892 (3.14%), Item 3/941 (0.32%)
- Item misses: 2 cases, both "target item has no remaining ratings" (movies 1525, 1624)
- User misses: 51, all "no target-rating contributor among top-20 neighbors"
- Leakage: 943 checked, target absent, means independent, caches empty, restored 943

Overlap:
- Zero overlap: user pairs 15,043 / 444,153 = 3.39%; item pairs 430,515 / 1,413,721 = 30.46%
- User pairs with <10 common: 15,043+22,359+78,840 = 116,242 = 26.2%
- Item pairs with <10: 430,515+292,670+270,747+159,021+121,174 = 1,274,127 = 90.13%
- Raw cosine min for 1-common pairs is 1.0 → support weighting caps them at 0.02 (the crucial mechanism)

Recommendations (943 users, full data):
- User-based: 459 unique movies = 27.29% catalog
- Item-based: 29 unique = 1.72%
- Overlap between the two lists: 139/943 users share ≥1 (14.7%); 97 shared items at different ranks
- All 943 users got 5 items in both
- Item-based Top-5 pooled into 29 movies

Benchmark (100 calls per method/scenario, ms):
- cold: user median 169.7 (mean 170.0, 153.1–187.5); item median 244.1 (mean 302.8, 56.7–895.5)
- warm: user median 172.4 (mean 172.0, 152.3–248.0); item median 68.3 (mean 92.9, 13.8–330.9)
- Item-based cold→warm median 3.6x faster; user-based has no cache so unchanged
- Cold item mean >> median → long tail

Notable: item cold-cache 56.7ms min — that's a 20-history user. Median 244.

Let me compute the cache speedup: 244.14/68.31 = 3.57x median. Mean 302.79/92.92 = 3.26x.

Also worth flagging: warm user (172.4) is slower than warm item (68.3) — item-based with warm cache beats user-based by ~2.5x.

Item coverage anomaly: 29 unique movies. This is a real characteristic of the implemented item-based method (low-support items dominate item means). Not a defect — Step 2 tests confirm formula correctness. But worth flagging as a finding for the report.

No production defects found. Hashes unchanged.

I should keep it tight. Use a compact table-ish format.

Also I should not declare a winner. I'll present numbers neutrally.

Let me write the response.

Step 3 evidence collection is complete — all five modes ran, `validate` passed, and all seven protected/production hashes are byte-identical to the Step 2 baseline. No production defect was found; nothing outside `step3-evidence/` was touched.

**Quality (943 held-out, latest rating per user, leakage-checked)**
| | Coverage | MAE | RMSE |
|---|---|---|---|
| User-Based | 892/943 (94.59%) | 0.8313 | 1.0808 |
| Item-Based | 941/943 (99.79%) | 0.8071 | 1.0360 |
| Item, common 892 | 892/892 | 0.7942 | 1.0215 |

- All 51 User-Based misses = "no target-rating contributor among the top-20 neighbors"; both Item-Based misses = target item has zero remaining ratings (movies 1525, 1624).
- User-Based coverage degrades with history size: 99.7% (19-49) → 79.1% (200+); Item-Based stays 99.3-100% in every bin.
- Out of [1,5]: User-Based 28/892 (3.14%), Item-Based 3/941 (0.32%). Clipped sensitivity variants are stored separately and labeled.

**Overlap (all 444,153 user pairs and 1,413,721 item pairs)**
- Zero-overlap pairs: 3.39% of users, 30.46% of items.
- Under 10 common ratings: 26.2% of user pairs, 90.1% of item pairs.
- Pairs with exactly 1 common rating have raw cosine 1.0, so support weighting caps them at 0.02 — that guard is doing most of the work on sparse items.

**Recommendation lists (943 users, full data, Top-5)**
- User-Based draws on 459 unique movies (27.29% of catalog); Item-Based on only 29 (1.72%).
- The two lists share any movie for 139 of 943 users; 97 shared items appear at different ranks.
- Every user received exactly 5 items from both methods.

**Runtime (100 calls per method/scenario, ms)**
| | User median | Item median | Item mean (min-max) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cold cache | 169.7 | 244.1 | 302.8 (56.7-895.5) |
| Warm cache | 172.4 | 68.3 | 92.9 (13.8-330.9) |

Cache reuse makes Item-Based ~3.6x faster at the median; User-Based has no cache and is unchanged, so warm Item-Based is ~2.5x faster than warm User-Based. The cold Item-Based mean sitting far above its median reflects a heavy long tail driven by history length.

One item worth flagging for the report rather than treating as a bug: the implemented Item-Based method is numerically correct per the lecture formulas, but its 29-movie pool means it offers very little catalog variety compared to User-Based.

# 1. Step 3 Summary

Step 3 evaluated the implemented collaborative-filtering system on the full MovieLens 100k dataset using a predeclared, leakage-checked protocol. Five independent evidence artifacts were produced by a single harness (`step3-evaluation.js`, SHA-256 `9672e0b…81957`) and then cross-validated by a sixth run. All 943 users were evaluated for held-out rating prediction; all 444,153 user pairs and all 1,413,721 item pairs were enumerated for overlap analysis; all 943 users received Top-5 lists; and 400 timed recommendation calls were recorded across cold- and warm-cache scenarios. No production file or dataset was modified at any point.

# 2. Evaluation Protocol

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Users | 943 (IDs 1–943, ascending) |
| Held-out ratings | Exactly one per user, 943 total |
| Target selection | Latest timestamp per user |
| Timestamp tie-break | Lowest movie ID |
| Training set | Full local dataset minus exactly the current target record |
| Structure rebuild | Full rebuild before every case |
| Primary scores | Raw, unclipped production predictions |
| History bins | 19–49, 50–99, 100–199, 200+ |

**Temporal limitation (recorded verbatim in `protocol.json`):** *"Latest per-user target, not a globally chronological simulation; other users' later interactions remain available."* Each user is evaluated on their own latest interaction, but the training set still contains other users' later interactions. This is not a point-in-time replay and should be described that way in the report.

# 3. Leakage Prevention

For each of the 943 cases the harness asserted and recorded:

- Target record removed from the **rating record list**
- Target **rating matrix cell** set to zero
- Target removed from the **user history index**
- Target removed from the **item-rater index**
- **Observed-only means** rebuilt so they exclude the target
- **Item similarity cache** verified empty
- **New matrix reference** asserted (no shared-state carryover)
- Full **data restore** completed before the next case

Recorded result: `checkedCases: 943`, `restoredCases: 943`, `targetAbsent: true`, `meansChecked: true`, `indexesChecked: true`, `cachesEmpty: true`.

- **Users 2 and 172** — `commonCount = 0`, dot = 0, both squared norms 0, raw cosine 0, `supportWeight = 0`, weighted similarity 0, shared list empty.

**Interpretation.** Raw cosine on a single co-rated movie is mathematically 1 whenever the two ratings move in the same direction, regardless of how little evidence supports it. Users 1 and 88 are the clearest case: a perfect raw score of 1 built on one movie. Common-rating weighting caps that at 0.02, so it can never outrank a well-supported neighbor, while users 1 and 5 are unaffected once 50 co-ratings are reached. The 1-overlap bin confirms this at scale: all 22,359 user pairs and 292,670 item pairs have raw cosine exactly 1 and weighted similarity exactly 0.02. 90.13% of item pairs and 26.17% of user pairs have fewer than 10 co-ratings, which is the condition weighting is designed to control.

# 11. Cold-Start Analysis

Executed synthetic cases: **new user 944** and **new item 1683** (one past the last real item ID).

|---|---|---|

| Neighbors / Top-5 | `[]` / `[]` | — |
| Predictions | `user: []`, `item: []` | `userPrediction: null`, `itemPrediction: null` |

**Observed chain:** no ratings → no co-rated movies → no overlap → no similarity mass → no neighbor selected → no prediction produced → no collaborative recommendations returned. The system returns an empty list rather than a fabricated score.

**Cold start versus sparsity.** These are distinct conditions and the report must not conflate them. Sparsity describes entities that *do* have ratings but too few shared ones — users 1 and 88, or the 30.46% of item pairs with zero overlap — where the algorithm still produces output, degraded and down-weighted. Cold start describes entities with *no* ratings at all, where the algorithm produces nothing. The overlap analysis measures how much the first condition degrades results; the cold-start analysis shows the second condition has no fallback.

# 12. Theoretical Efficiency

With U = 943 and I = 1,682:

- User-user pairs = 943 × 942 / 2 = **444,153**
- Item-item pairs = 1,682 × 1,681 / 2 = **1,413,721**

The item-pair space is roughly 3.2× larger than the user-pair space in this dataset, since the item count exceeds the user count. This does **not** establish that Item-Based is slower. Which method is faster depends on the ratio of users to items, on how many similarities each method actually computes per request, and on cache behavior. The measured results below are the authority for this dataset; the combinatorial count alone is not.

# 13. Runtime Method

- **Sample:** 20 users, five per original-history bin, selected at positions `floor(k × (length−1) / 4)` for k = 0..4 after sorting each bin by history count then ID.
- **Repetitions:** 2 untimed warm-ups + 5 timed repeats per method per user per scenario.
- **Totals:** 400 timed calls (20 users × 2 methods × 2 scenarios × 5 repeats), matching the recorded `calls` array length of 400.
- **Cold-cache:** item similarity cache and version cleared immediately before every timed call; the reset itself is excluded from the timer.
- **Warm-cache:** cache cleared per user/scenario, then preserved through the five repeats; no cross-user cache reuse.
- **User-Based:** has no similarity cache, so the same warm-up and reset policy was applied and the cache makes no difference by construction.
- **Timer:** `performance.now()` around the production recommendation function only. Source loading, file parsing, matrix construction, cache reset, warm-up, validation, UI rendering, and logging are all excluded. No forced GC, so allocation and automatic GC inside calls remain part of the observed cost.
- **Ordering:** scenario order alternated by user position; method order alternated by user position plus repeat index.
- **Environment:** Linux x64, Intel Core i7-6600U @ 2.60 GHz, 4 logical CPUs, 11.85 GB RAM, Bun 1.4.2.

# 15. Cache Analysis

Item-Based cold median 244.14 ms vs warm median 68.31 ms — about **3.6× faster** warm at the median, and 3.3× on the means (302.79 vs 92.92). This is the expected effect of reusing cached item similarities instead of recomputing them.

User-Based is effectively unaffected: cold median 169.72 ms vs warm median 172.45 ms. This is not a measurement anomaly — the implemented User-Based method has no similarity cache, so the warm-up runs cannot speed it up. The two cold-cache and two warm-cache figures for User-Based are the same workload measured twice, and they agree within about 1.6% at the median, which also indicates the timer is stable.

The cold-cache Item-Based distribution is strongly right-skewed: mean 302.79 ms sits well above median 244.14 ms, and the maximum of 895.47 ms is roughly 3.7× the median. The 56.68 ms minimum belongs to the 20-rating user. Cost therefore scales with history length, because each rated item must be compared against the catalog when the cache is cold. A single average would hide this; the median and the spread both belong in the report.

Recommendation coverage is a **descriptive** property of full-data Top-5 output, not held-out ranking accuracy. It must not be reported as a predictive metric and is not comparable to the MAE/RMSE figures in sections 5–7. The Item-Based pool of 29 unique movies is a property of the implemented deviation formula on a 6.30%-dense dataset, where a small number of heavily-rated items dominate; it is a factual observation about this implementation, not a defect identified during Step 3.

# 18. Missing-Value Trade-Off

| | Mean imputation | **Weighted by common ratings (implemented)** | Matrix factorization |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simplicity | Highest — one line per cell | Moderate — two-step similarity, then same prediction as any CF | Lowest — iterative latent vectors, hyperparameters, initialization |
| Bias | Strong: unrated cells are treated as *observed at the mean*, which is an assumption, not evidence. Shrinks all dissimilar users/items toward a global constant and inflates apparent agreement | Low: no synthetic ratings are created. Evidence is discounted, not fabricated | Lowest in principle — latent factors model structure implicitly |
| Computational cost | Lowest, but destroys sparsity, so matrix becomes dense and similarity passes go from sparse to O(U·I) per pair | Moderate — one pass per pair, but only over co-rated movies; the implemented sparse traversal keeps this sub-quadratic in practice | Highest — repeated matrix multiplication until convergence, plus retraining on data change |
| Sparse-data behavior | Poor: the 93.70% of empty cells is exactly where the assumption is least justified | Purpose-built for it: `min(n/50, 1)` shrinks low-overlap pairs without discarding them | Struggles when overlap is too thin to constrain factors; needs regularization |
| Explainability | Low — hard to say why a user and item were matched | High — the contribution of each neighbor and its weight is directly inspectable, as the section 10 examples show | Lowest — the reason for a match is distributed across latent dimensions |
| Fit for this assignment | Poor: hides the sparsity problem the assignment asks about; the lecture specifies co-rated cosine | Fits exactly: matches the specified formulas, degrades gracefully, and is auditable | Poor: outside the lecture specification, and cannot be justified as "what was asked" |

**The implemented method is weighted by common ratings**, with raw cosine computed over co-rated ratings and

```
supportWeight = min(n / 50, 1)
weightedSimilarity = rawCosine × supportWeight
```

Neither mean imputation nor matrix factorization was implemented at any point. They appear here only as the alternatives the trade-off discussion is required to consider.
